title: Contracts & Instruments
hook: MNQ. MGC. Know what you're trading before you trade it.
mission: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain the difference between the instrument you trade and the size you trade it at.

blocks.heading: The instrument is the market. The contract count is your size inside it.

beats.heading: Same market, different weight
beats.body: MNQ, NQ, MGC, ES are instruments — they tell you what market you're trading. 1 contract, 2 contracts, 5 contracts tells you how much exposure you have to that instrument's move.

beats.heading: Micros keep you teachable
beats.body: Smaller exposure gives you room to actually learn before your emotions hijack the lesson.

blocks.heading: MNQ vs MGC — same 10-point move, different dollars
blocks.prompt: Tap each instrument to see its per-point value.

left.label: MNQ
left.desc: MNQ moves $2 for every point. A 10-point move = $20.

right.label: MGC
right.desc: MGC moves $10 for every point — 5x MNQ's weight on the same 10-point move.

left.label: Instrument
points: What market you're trading (MNQ, MGC, ES)
Doesn't change no matter how many contracts you hold

right.label: Contract count
points: How much exposure you have to that instrument

questions.question: A trader switches from trading 1 contract of MNQ to 5 contracts of MNQ. Has she changed instruments?
options: No — she's still trading MNQ; only her size and dollar exposure changed
Yes — 5 contracts makes it a different instrument
It's impossible to tell without knowing the price
questions.why: The instrument stays MNQ — contract count only changes exposure.

questions.question: Two traders both say they're "trading MNQ." One holds 1 contract, the other holds 20. Are they taking the same risk?
options: No — 20 contracts moves 20x the money on the same point move as 1 contract
Yes — same instrument means same risk
It depends only on which broker they use
questions.why: Same instrument, very different dollar risk — contract count is what changes exposure.

takeaways: The instrument tells you what market you're trading — not how much you're risking.
Contract count is the multiplier that turns a point move into real dollars.
A small instrument can still carry big risk if the size is large enough.
remember: Same market. Different emotional and dollar weight.
